IRIS is mentioned only as heritage for the Polstar modulator rotary mechanism, and on the secondary mirror mechanism (IRIS/SUVI). No IRIS data, synthetic observables, or IRIS instrument description are given.
IRIS cited only as background: prior O IV/S IV diagnostics near 1400 A applied to IRIS data (De Pontieu et al. 2014) and Polito et al. 2016. The authors analyze no IRIS data.
The data analyzed are Hinode/EIS spectra and SDO/AIA images, with no IRIS data or synthetic IRIS-band observables. The synthetic O IV spectrum covers 160-300 A, outside the IRIS windows.
IRIS appears only in the name of the coordinated campaign, IRIS-Hinode Operation Plan (IHOP) 455. No IRIS data are analyzed or shown; the data come from EIS, SPICE, AIA and EUI.

IRIS appears only as background: the ATLCW model's construction used the Mg II k profile observed with IRIS. The authors analyze only ALMA and Metsähovi data and compute no synthetic IRIS observables.

IRIS (De Pontieu et al. 2014) appears only in background/introduction as an example of UV spectroscopy. The paper's synthetic Fe II spectra at 250-278 nm fall outside the IRIS coverage, so no synthetic-observable tag applies.
IRIS appears only as a citation (De Pontieu et al. 2014) in a list of missions whose data could be combined with CHASE. No IRIS data, synthetic observables, or IRIS instrument description are given.
IRIS Mg II comparison with ALMA is only background citing da Silva Santos et al. (2020); no IRIS data are analyzed.
IRIS appears only as a comparison with published results (Carlsson et al. 2019) on Mg II line widths. The synthetic Ca II and mm continuum lie outside the IRIS coverage.
OBSERVATIONAL_DATA: authors use full-disk IRIS mosaics (2013-2017) to measure disk-averaged C II 1334/1335 emission correlation and ratio for the Sun, compared with HAT-P-11.

IRIS (De Pontieu et al. 2014) is cited only as a solar observatory that adopted a Yohkoh/SXT-style dynamic exposure control; this is background, and no IRIS data or synthetic IRIS observables are analyzed.

Simulated light curves are normalized to Si IV 1394/1403 flux, but the SPARCS NUV/FUV broadband photometric passbands (153-171 nm, 258-308 nm) are not IRIS spectrograph windows or slit-jaw channels, so this is not a synthetic IRIS observable.
IRIS is only listed in Table 4 as a coordinated data set (IHOP 421) for the MaGIXS flight; no IRIS data are analyzed or shown.
The acknowledgments thank IRIS for coordinated observations during launch, and the paper does not use those data.

IRIS (De Pontieu et al. 2014) appears only in the introduction as one of several new instruments. The paper is a review of coronal seismology data analysis techniques for EUV imaging, with no IRIS data or IRIS-band synthetic observables.

IRIS (garbled as 'solar interface layer spectrometer') is mentioned only in the background as an instrument that uses the KLL flat-field method; the paper analyzes FY-3E/X-EUVI data only, with no IRIS data or synthetic observables.
IRIS appears only as background: Tian et al. (2016) is cited for a QPP event seen in the Fe XXI 1354 line. The authors analyze VLA, RHESSI, Fermi/GBM and SDO data, not IRIS data.
IRIS appears only as a citation of Polito et al. Fe XXI results in the background discussion; the authors analyze no IRIS data.
IRIS is named only as an example of rastering slit spectroscopy at Lyman-alpha wavelengths, which motivates a new instrument concept.

IRIS appears only as a background citation (De Pontieu et al. 2021) in the introduction, among space observatories that have studied solar flares. The paper analyzes GWAC, TESS, K2, LAMOST and Gaia data, and no IRIS data or synthetic observables.
IRIS is cited only as background: Polito et al. (2018) detected Fe XXI Doppler shifts with IRIS. The paper uses Hinode/EIS, AIA and RHESSI data and no IRIS data or synthetic observables.
IRIS appears only as a citation of Panesar et al. (2018b), who used IRIS UV images to study jetlets; the authors neither analyze nor show IRIS data (background/comparison with published results).

IRIS (De Pontieu et al. 2014) is mentioned only as a future-work suggestion for multi-instrument inversions with Mg II and Si IV. The paper uses no IRIS data and synthesizes only Ca II lines, which are outside the IRIS coverage.
IRIS appears only as background: Gosic et al. (2018) compared SST cancellations with IRIS data (De Pontieu et al. 2014). The authors analyze SST/CRISP data only and show no IRIS data.
IRIS appears only as background: Pereira et al. (2014) used IRIS Mg II and Si IV lines to observe Type II spicules. The authors show no IRIS data.
IRIS is cited again only to compare with published spicule results (Pereira 2014, Skogsrud 2015). The paper's own data are from Solar Orbiter EUI, SDO/AIA and HMI, and SPICE.
IRIS (De Pontieu et al. 2014) appears only in a background list of past solar missions, with no IRIS data, synthetic observables, or instrument description.

IRIS is cited only as background: Kohutova et al. (2020) used AIA and IRIS data. The authors analyze Solar Orbiter EUI, PHI and SPICE data, not IRIS data, and compute no synthetic IRIS observables.
IRIS is mentioned only in a summary of the earlier Paper IV, which used IRIS whole-Sun scans. This paper analyzes HST COS/STIS, Chandra and TESS data, not IRIS data.
IRIS appears only as a background reference to Paper IV's finding about spatially resolved Si IV. The authors do not analyze or show IRIS data.
